title: THEMIS: a framework for cost-benefit analysis of COVID-19 non-pharmaceutical interventions
contribution: A modular, open-source system-dynamics framework that simulates the COVID-19 epidemic under any sequence of NPIs with the group's DELPHI model, prices five humanitarian and economic cost dimensions, and compares all 216 first-wave policies with the policy actually implemented in six regions.
problem_entry: {AP DA; SD as simulator} NPIs cut transmission but carry economic and humanitarian costs; earlier cost-benefit studies priced only the implemented policy or compared two NPIs mostly by GDP, so the paper costs any region's actual NPI sequence against a wide range of alternatives using the realized pandemic (abstract; pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A policy is an NPI sequence with switching dates; DELPHI turns it into an epidemic path through a region-specific, piecewise-constant reduction of the infection rate, effects of untried NPIs are imputed by regressing regional on global effects, five cost modules price the path, and all 6^3 = 216 three-month policies are enumerated (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: 11-state SEIR-type DELPHI with under-detection, an arctan-plus-resurgence response and declining mortality (pp. 3-4, 15-16); parameter counts disagree, 7 calibrated plus 9 fitted (p. 4) against 13 fitted per area (p. 16); NPI data from 167 regions in March-April 2020, first wave 15 March-15 June 2020, six regions with sourced cost parameters (pp. 7-9, 17-18); admitted simplifications: linear and additive costs (p. 11), depression only under the two severe NPIs (pp. 6, 8), GDP without government spending and net exports (p. 7).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs): closed-form cost formulas for QALYs lost, hospital/ICU/ventilator days, depression and PTSD, GDP and unemployment on a simulated trajectory (eqs. 5-14, pp. 6-7)
linear regression of region-specific on global NPI effects to impute untried NPIs, reused for GDP and unemployment effects (Fig. 3, p. 5; p. 7)
exhaustive enumeration of 216 policies instead of an optimization model (p. 8)
DELPHI fit by recency-weighted MSE, TNC daily within 20% bounds and dual annealing weekly within 50% bounds (p. 16)
experiments: Six regions (Germany, New York State, Florida, Spain, Singapore, Brazil), all 216 policies plotted in a humanitarian-economic cost plane with the actual policy marked (Fig. 4, pp. 8-9) and the 20 cheapest decomposed (Fig. 5, p. 10); flat frontier with economic cost at 10-30% of GDP (p. 8); 6-6-6 never the total-cost optimum (p. 9); New York far from the frontier (about $120 billion humanitarian and $4 billion economic saving possible), Germany close to it (pp. 8-9); no validation of the counterfactuals; the introduction's 90%-cost-cut-for-one-week-earlier claim (p. 2) has no matching experiment in pp. 7-11.
positioning: Set against cost-benefit studies of the implemented policy only (Broughel and Kotrous 2021) or of two NPIs with GDP emphasis (Layard et al. 2020; Shlomai et al. 2021); builds on the group's DELPHI model and clinical-outcomes database (pp. 2-4).
writing: Three numbered implications and two contributions in the introduction (pp. 2-3); results narrated region by region with currency figures (pp. 8-11); a separate limitations section with four concrete limits (p. 11); a headline intro claim (90% cost cut, p. 2) not backed by a reported experiment.
limits_future: Only historically implemented NPIs can be evaluated, residual confounding likely, SEIR models need large populations, costs linear and additive (p. 11); the developing-country conclusion rests on Spain and Brazil (pp. 10-11); future work is a generic call for further research on how NPIs and other levers interact (p. 11).

method_links.note: The owner's actual policy is the baseline in every region, decisions are scored by their costs rather than by forecast accuracy, and the evaluation's limits are printed; not met: no field test, and DELPHI is called highly accurate (p. 4) without the field's metric, where the SKILL's correction applies (relative WIS 0.99 against the naive 1.00, 05 section 5.2).
A per-region price curve between humanitarian and economic cost is published, but it comes from enumerating 216 policies, with no single knob and no solution-independent bound.
A separate limitations section names four concrete limits.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: counterfactual replay against the historical decision-maker
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The first wave is replayed under all 216 alternative policies and each region's actually implemented policy is marked in the same cost plane.
Alternatives are limited to mobility NPIs actually used somewhere in March-April 2020, so no alternative relies on information unavailable at the time.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: deployed forecaster reused as the policy simulator
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: DELPHI, built for forecasting and used in the CDC's central ensemble, becomes the counterfactual engine of a prescriptive cost-benefit analysis.

transferable: Limit counterfactual alternatives to actions that were actually taken somewhere at the time, and say so, so the comparison does not reward hindsight (p. 8).

Impute the effect of an action a region never took by regressing the region's observed effects on the global effects of the actions it did take; reuse the same map for secondary outcomes such as GDP and unemployment (Fig. 3, p. 5; p. 7).
Drop outcome components confounded by concurrent policies (government spending, net exports) and state why (p. 7).
Plot the whole enumerated policy set in a two-cost plane with the actual decision highlighted, so the frontier and the decision-maker's implied trade-off are visible (Fig. 4, pp. 8-9).
For a non-convex ODE fit, weight recent errors by t^2/T^2, balance cases against deaths, run a local solver daily within 20% bounds and a global one weekly within 50% bounds (p. 16).
coauthors: Michael Lingzhi Li (MIT ORC; PhD 2022, postdoc 2022-2023 per 04-mentorship.md), Saksham Soni (MIT Sloan)

quotes.text: In fact, across all countries tested, the most severe policy, 6-6-6, is never the optimal policy in terms of achieving minimum costs in the sum of the two dimensions.
However, despite these measures, it is likely that residual confounding remains.

title: Learning Sparse Nonlinear Dynamics via Mixed-Integer Optimization
contribution: MIOSR, an exact SOS-1 mixed-integer formulation of SINDy's sparsity-constrained regression, solved to certified optimality in seconds and shown on nine canonical ODE and PDE systems to recover sparser, more accurate dynamics than the field's heuristics with less data and under constraints (arXiv v1 read).
problem_entry: {ML; IO as engine} SINDy's equation discovery runs on heuristic sparse regression (thresholded least squares and relaxations) that misses small coefficients and resists constraints; the paper claims such heuristics are unnecessary and inadequate, citing an over-a-trillion-fold MIO speed-up since 1990 (abstract; pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Per state dimension, ridge regression with a hard cardinality constraint modelled by SOS-1 sets and binaries, written in Gram form so the model size is independent of n, with a block-diagonal joint model when physical constraints couple coordinates (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Polynomial libraries; additive Gaussian noise as a percentage of the data norm; 50 random initial conditions; 2/3-1/3 train-validation split with AICc (pp. 5-6); weak form for noise and PDEs (pp. 3, 10-13); general-purpose solvers limited to a few thousand SOS-1 constraints, enough for libraries up to a few hundred terms (p. 4).
proof_devices: no theorems; optimality certified by the solver's dual bound (p. 2)
SOS-1 support constraints instead of big-M, because coefficient bounds are costly and do not carry over to extra constraints (p. 4)
Gram-form objective making the MIO size independent of the number of samples (eqs. 13-15, p. 4)
block-diagonal joint model with linear equalities from a potential function for physical constraints (eq. 16, pp. 5, 10)
hard constraint rather than penalty, justified by statistical properties under collinearity (p. 4)
experiments: Lorenz, Hopf, MHD, 2D Duffing, Van der Pol, Lotka-Volterra, Rossler, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky and reaction-diffusion (pp. 7-13); baselines STLSQ, SR3, SSR, ensembled STLSQ only (LASSO, probabilistic and deep methods excluded, p. 6); Gurobi 9.5.0, one core, 30 s per dimension (pp. 5-6); support IoU, coefficient error, derivative RMSE over 50 trials in log space (pp. 6-7); MIOSR wins with little data, small coefficients, large libraries (pp. 7-8), often faster as n grows and up to 100x faster on a laptop (p. 9); breaks down at very high noise (p. 12), no gain for small libraries (pp. 13-14); PDE runs tuned with the known truth (p. 13); all synthetic; certification rate not reported; code public (p. 5).
positioning: Against SINDy's thresholded least squares and its successors (SR3, conditional gradients, greedy and convex relaxations) (p. 1); built on Bertsimas-King-Mazumder 2016 and the group's scalable sparse-regression line (p. 2); a PySINDy-compatible implementation to join the community's toolchain (p. 2).
writing: Four bold-labelled contributions (p. 2); the field's intractability sentence quoted in order 'to directly dispel' it (p. 8); a confident close that MIOSR should be the default optimizer (p. 14) next to printed failure regimes (pp. 12-14).
limits_future: Scale limited to a few thousand SOS-1 constraints (p. 4); breakdown at very high noise (p. 12); no benefit for small libraries with similar coefficients (pp. 13-14); synthetic systems only (pp. 7-13); future: control and implicit-equation SINDy variants and better data preparation (pp. 12, 14).

method_links.note: One MIO replaces greedy thresholding, with stated time limit, solver version and machine, a dual-bound certificate, a duel against the community's incumbents on known-truth systems, and where it wins and loses; partial: warm starts only suggested, certification rate missing, no real data.

The why-now figure (over a trillion-fold MIO speed-up since 1990) is borrowed from three surveys, not rebuilt; the paper does time its own class on two machines, meeting half of the SKILL's correction.
A problem owned by system identification is written exactly as an MIQO that stays in the solver class, with the scale boundary printed.
High-noise breakdown, the PDE converse and the smaller edge with tight libraries are printed in the body.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The MIOSR implementation adheres to the PySINDy interface, computationally and conceptually, so it fits existing preprocessing, library and outer-loop tools.
For PDEs every method is given hyperparameters set from the known truth, to ask whether recovery is possible at all and separate optimizer failure from model-selection failure.

transferable: Write an l0-constrained least-squares objective in Gram form so the MIO does not grow with n; more data then tightens bounds and can shorten solves (pp. 4, 9).
Prefer SOS-1 to big-M when coefficient bounds are unknown or constraints will be added, and state the scale it costs (p. 4).
Fit coordinates separately unless a constraint couples them; then switch to one block-diagonal joint model (pp. 4-5).
Randomize initial conditions instead of the field's usual fixed one, and average errors in log space so one outlier cannot dominate (pp. 5, 7).
Time the exact method on two hardware configurations to show its parallel headroom (p. 9; Fig. 7, p. 19).
coauthors: Wes Gurnee (MIT ORC; thesis record 2025 per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: For system identification problems, we claim that such relaxations and heuristics are unnecessary, and ultimately, inadequate.
At very high levels of noise, MIOSR starts to break down, converging to the approximate performance of heuristic methods.

title: Sparse plus low rank matrix decomposition: A discrete optimization approach
contribution: An exact rank- and cardinality-constrained, ridge-regularized formulation of sparse-plus-low-rank decomposition with an alternating-minimization heuristic scaling to n = 10,000, a perspective-based semidefinite relaxation that certifies it (n = 200 in hours), and a custom branch-and-bound solving n <= 25 to near-optimality.
problem_entry: {ML; IO and CP as engines} Robust PCA is solved by convex surrogates or non-convex heuristics whose guarantees need incoherence or a basin of attraction, and the only exact method reported no optimal solutions at n = 10; the paper keeps rank and l0 constraints explicit and seeks solutions plus certified bounds (pp. 2-5).
key_idea: Alternate closed-form truncated-SVD and hard-threshold steps for good solutions; lift support to binaries and column space to a projection matrix, add perspective constraints and convex hulls for an SDP bound; combine both in branch-and-bound over sparsity patterns (pp. 8-11, 15, 22-23).
assumptions: Square data matrix, given target rank and sparsity, lambda and mu > 0 (otherwise the relaxation bound is 0) (pp. 2, 15); Theorem 12's regularization and singular-value-ratio conditions called easy to verify (p. 12); synthetic data only: Gaussian low-rank factors, symmetric sparse U(-5,5) corruptions, Gaussian noise (p. 24).
proof_devices: regularization equals robustness to adversarial data perturbations, extending Bertsimas-Copenhaver 2018 to matrices (Propositions 3-4, p. 7)
iteration bound for alternating minimization from the starting objective and the unconstrained minimum (Proposition 10, p. 11)
alternating minimization on a fixed support equals projected gradient descent, importing linear convergence from Ha et al. 2020 (Proposition 11, Theorem 12, pp. 12-13)
projection-matrix and binary lifting with perspective constraints and convex hulls for an SDP relaxation (eqs. 18-20, Theorem 15, p. 15)
hidden convexity of the low-rank subproblem (Theorem 16, p. 16)
dominance over Lee-Zou's relaxation by a feasible-point map plus a strict 2x2 instance (Propositions 17-18, pp. 17-18)
reverse-Huber penalty reading; the unregularized big-M relaxation equals Lasso plus nuclear norm (Proposition 19, eqs. 27-28, pp. 18-19)
finite termination and epsilon-optimality of branch-and-bound (Theorems 21-22, pp. 22-23)
experiments: Julia 1.5.2, JuMP 0.21.7, Mosek 9.2 on MIT Supercloud, up to 192 GB (pp. 23-24); 30-fold block cross-validation (pp. 24-25); baselines GoDec, S-PCP, fRPCA, AccAltProj (authors' MATLAB), ScaledGD (p. 24); Algorithm 1 lower errors in most trials at comparable time up to n = 10,000 (pp. 25-28), ScaledGD better on sparse-support discovery at high dimension and on low-rank error in 3 trials (pp. 28, 34); relaxation gaps up to n = 140 at up to 14,731 s, unit not stated (Table 3, p. 48); branch-and-bound with 5% tolerance solves n <= 25, hardest 14,709 nodes in 28,977 s (Table 1, p. 33); synthetic data only.
positioning: Critiques S-PCP (memory at n = 200, incoherence), GoDec and Burer-Monteiro-type methods (unverifiable assumptions), and Lee-Zou's weak bound (pp. 3-5); extends Bertsimas-Copenhaver's regularization-robustness result (p. 7); applies the group's matrix-perspective machinery (p. 15).
writing: Three-part contribution list (methodological, algorithmic, computational) (pp. 2-3); scaling of all three algorithms stated in the abstract (p. 1); four numbered experimental questions answered in a summary section (pp. 24, 33-35).
limits_future: An SDP at every node is the bottleneck (p. 33); branch-and-bound time goes mostly to certification and improves Algorithm 1 only marginally (p. 36); no real data despite listed applications (pp. 1, 24); future: second-order-cone bounds per node and alternative branching rules (p. 36).

method_links.note: Heuristic, then a relaxation certificate, then exact branch-and-bound, dueling named incumbents with versions stated and losses to ScaledGD printed; variant parts: synthetic data only and a custom branch-and-bound instead of a commercial MIO solver.
The discrete problem is stated exactly and relaxed within the semidefinite class; each algorithm's size boundary is printed (n = 10,000, 200, 25).
The ridge regularizer is shown to be robustness against adversarial perturbations of the data matrix, offered as of independent interest to the RO community.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: rival method as a relaxation of the exact formulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Lee-Zou's relaxation is dominated (weakly in general, strictly on a 2x2 instance), and the Lasso-plus-nuclear-norm problem is shown to be the unregularized big-M relaxation of the exact model.

With enough ridge regularization, alternating minimization on a fixed support converges linearly to the global optimum, so enumerating supports is exact; the paper calls it a phase transition in difficulty.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: exact optimum on a small solvable instance as the certificate for a heuristic
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Branch-and-bound solves n <= 25 to within 5% and shows the heuristic's solution is only marginally improvable.

transferable: Lift rank to a projection matrix and support to binaries, then convexify with perspective constraints and the convex hull of projection matrices (p. 15).
Prove relaxation dominance in two steps: a feasible-point map to show it is at least as strong, then one small explicit instance where it is strictly stronger (pp. 17-18).
Bound alternating-minimization iterations by the ratio of the starting objective to the unconstrained minimum (Proposition 10, p. 11).
On a fixed discrete pattern, recast block-coordinate updates as projected gradient descent and inherit its convergence theorem (pp. 12-13).
Cross-validate a matrix decomposition by holding out a random l-by-l block and scoring its reconstruction from the other blocks (pp. 24-25).
Report branch-and-bound per instance as root gap, nodes and time, and say where the time goes (pp. 32-33, 36).
coauthors: Ryan Cory-Wright (Imperial College Business School; his PhD 2022 per 04-mentorship.md), Nicholas A. G. Johnson (MIT; Johnson 2024 in the ML thesis lineage of 01-publications.md)

quotes.text: Our heuristic scales to n = 10000 in minutes and our convex relaxation scales to n = 200 in hours.
This implies that the final solution returned by Algorithm 2 is, in general, only marginally better than the solution returned by Algorithm 1.

title: The power and limits of predictive approaches to observational data-driven optimization: The case of pricing
contribution: Shows that optimal decisions are not identifiable from observational data, bounds the true-profit loss of predictive (plug-in) pricing under confounding, and builds a consistent hypothesis test of decision optimality that, on auto-loan data, rejects predictive pricing in most segments while a parametric propensity-score approach recoups 36-70% of the lost profit (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: {DA; AP} Transactional data confound decision and outcome, yet practice optimizes the best prediction of reward given the decision; since only the final decision's objective matters, the paper asks when predictive decisions are near-optimal and how to test it, opening with two data-consistent models that recommend different prices (pp. 1-10).
key_idea: Power: bound R(z~)/R(z*) for pricing through the confounding error and pricing structure; limits: test H0: R(z*) = R(z^) with a non-parametric partial-means kernel estimator under ignorability, a chi-square null and a bootstrap scale; plus a generalized-propensity-score parametric method (pp. 10-26).
assumptions: Pricing with profit z - c, univariate price, linear non-increasing mean demand (p. 12); bounds add confounding size relative to market (Thm 2), joint normality with non-positive correlation (Thm 3, p. 13) or non-increasing confounding (Thm 4, p. 14); the test needs root-n convergent decision rules, ignorability given covariates and kernel/optimality/distribution regularity (Assumptions 1-5, pp. 15, 18, 21-22); simulated data and Columbia CPRM auto-loan data in 16 segments (pp. 16, 27-31).
proof_devices: non-identifiability by a constructed counterexample of two data-consistent demand models (Example 1, Theorem 1, pp. 7-10)
sandwiching the predictive maximizer between maximizers under extremal confounding (proof of Theorem 2, p. 36)
bound in an estimable quantity, average demand over market size, under a distributional assumption (Theorem 3, p. 13)
bounds checked against worked curves: 0.71 <= 0.75, 0.94 <= 0.96, 0.79 <= 0.84 (pp. 11-14)
asymptotic normality of the kernel estimate and decision, chi-square null law of the test statistic, bootstrap estimate of the scale (Theorems 6-8, pp. 22-24)
generalized propensity score suffices for identification (Theorem 9, p. 25)
experiments: Simulated example: predictive price earns zero true profit against an optimum of 31.25 (p. 28); 256 replicates, the test reaches nominal 5% size after a few hundred observations (p. 29); auto loans, B = 100 bootstrap draws, n = 690-4,495 per segment: non-parametric predictive rejected at p < 0.05 in 13 of 16 segments, parametric predictive in 9, prescriptive parametric passes in all but 2 and recoups 70% or 36% of lost profit (pp. 30-32); software and run times not reported in the pages read.
positioning: Extends Besbes, Phillips and Zeevi (2010)'s objective-optimality test from experimental to observational data and causal effects, reproducing their auto-loan study and refuting its evidence while agreeing with its conclusion (pp. 14, 29-32); uses Rosenbaum-Rubin ignorability and Hirano-Imbens generalized propensity scores (pp. 17, 25).
writing: A toy demand table and a two-consultant parable open the argument (pp. 4, 7-9); 'all models are wrong but some models are useful' framing (p. 3); every bound checked on a worked example (pp. 11-14); power-and-limits framing carried from title to conclusion (pp. 1, 32-33).
limits_future: Bounds only for linear-demand pricing (p. 12); the test needs ignorability, argued not tested for the auto-loan data (pp. 15-18, 31); residual endogeneity needs instruments (pp. 18-19); future: similar bounds for other observational decision problems via problem structure (p. 12).

method_links.note: Decisions are scored by the true objective, not model fit; the incumbent study's own methods, data and segments are the baseline; the incumbent's evidence is refuted while its conclusion is accepted.

The price of predicting under confounding is an optimality-ratio curve in one knob (Fig. 2), but the knob is neither known nor estimable, so Theorem 3 moves to an estimable ratio; no decision-maker sets the knob.
Weak, metadata only: arXiv v1 May 2016 and v2 May 2017, journal version 2023 per the index; the manuscript stayed in circulation for years.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: assume only what can be estimated, worst-case the rest
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 3 replaces the unknowable confounding size by average demand relative to market size, which can be unbiasedly and consistently estimated.
Two consultants' complete demand models both reproduce the observed price-demand distribution yet recommend different prices; adding a covariate and ignorability selects one.
The test asks whether a decision rule's true objective is distinguishable from optimal, not whether the demand model fits.

transferable: To prove non-identifiability, build two models that reproduce the observed joint distribution exactly but imply different optimal decisions (Table 2, pp. 7-9).
Bound a plug-in decision's true-objective ratio by sandwiching its maximizer between the maximizers under extremal model error (Theorem 2, pp. 12, 36).
Check every bound against a worked instance whose true ratio is known (pp. 11-14).
Test decision rules, not models: the estimated objective gap between the estimated optimum and the rule's decision, calibrated by its asymptotic law with a bootstrapped scale (pp. 23-24).
Re-run the incumbent study on its own data and segments, then add the segments it left out (pp. 29-30).
coauthors: Nathan Kallus (Cornell Tech; PhD 2015, postdoc 2015-2016 per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: for optimization purposes it is only the objective value of the final decision that matters, rather than the validity of any model used to arrive at it.
It is clear that this approach leaves much revenue on the table.

title: A new perspective on low-rank optimization
contribution: The Matrix Perspective Reformulation Technique: projection matrices model rank as binaries model support, and matrix perspectives of spectral regularizers give semidefinite relaxations that are convex hulls of basic low-rank sets, yielding stronger and often faster bounds for reduced-rank regression, NMF and D-optimal design (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: {CP; IO as source technique; ML applications} Low-rank problems have efficient heuristics but almost no strong lower bounds, while in MIO the perspective reformulation made best-subset relaxations near-exact; the paper builds the matrix analog, motivated by best subset versus reduced-rank regression (pp. 1-4).
key_idea: Model rank with an orthogonal projection matrix (X = YX, tr Y <= k), replace a spectral regularizer by the trace of its matrix perspective, and relax Y to {0 <= Y <= I, tr Y <= k}: the perspective technique with projection matrices for binaries (pp. 10-14).
assumptions: Linear objective plus trace of a matrix-convex operator function plus rank penalty or constraint over a proper cone with linear constraints; omega grows super-linearly (Assumptions 1 and 3, pp. 2, 6, 12-13); synthetic instances only in section 5 (pp. 25-30).
proof_devices: equivalence of the projection and perspective forms via commuting matrices and eigenvalue reduction to the scalar perspective (Theorem 1, Proposition 4, pp. 13-14)
convex hull of {tr f(X) + mu rank X <= t, rank X <= k} by projecting Y onto the commutant of X and invoking Gunluk-Linderoth's vector hull (Theorem 2, pp. 14-15)
corollaries giving convex hulls for matrix-completion and D-optimal-design substructures (pp. 21, 24)
closure of the matrix perspective for rank-deficient arguments (Proposition 3, p. 11; proof in the unread appendix)
experiments: Julia 1.5, JuMP 0.21.6, Mosek 9.1, one Xeon core with 32 GB, code public (p. 25); reduced-rank regression: the stronger relaxation recovers the true rank with better accuracy than the nuclear norm, 1-2 orders faster, about twice the size within 120 GB and 12 h (pp. 25-26); NMF: ALS solutions certified 0-3% optimal (p. 28); D-optimal design: gaps 0-3% for k <= 7 against >= 88.8% for the Boolean relaxation, two orders slower, 28.43% at k = 9; Table 3 caption contradicts the text on n and m (pp. 29-30).
positioning: Generalizes MIO's perspective reformulation (Stubbs; Frangioni-Gentile; Akturk et al.; Gunluk-Linderoth) and the authors' mixed-projection framework (pp. 2-3); borrows the matrix perspective from operator theory (p. 10); classifies prior work as heuristics, relax-and-round and exact methods (p. 4).
writing: Motivating example built as an explicit vector-to-matrix analogy, called striking (pp. 2-4); two-part contribution statement (p. 5); thanks referees for the function's name and a refined definition (p. 31).
limits_future: Completely positive cone intractable, doubly non-negative surrogate without effective rounding (pp. 24-25); D-optimal relaxation useless when k >= n (p. 24); quantum relative entropy cones expensive (p. 30); open: weaker conditions than matrix convexity (p. 14); future: automatic MPRT detection in solvers, SDP-free algorithms, custom branching for exact solves at scale (p. 31).

method_links.note: Rank problems are written exactly with projection matrices and relaxed within the semidefinite class; boundaries are printed (completely positive cone, k >= n, solve times).
The relaxation certifies existing heuristics (ALS, greedy rounding) with reported gaps, but there is no exact solve and no duel on real data.
The why-now is qualitative (recent advances in algorithmic theory and computational power), with no rebuilt figure.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: subsume the incumbent as a special case
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The technique generalizes MIO's perspective reformulation, and the sparse-regression relaxation of the paper's ref. [25] is its diagonal case.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: projection matrices as the binaries of rank
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Rank is modelled by an orthogonal projection matrix and strengthened by a matrix perspective, transplanting the binary-plus-perspective device of MIO; reused in S218 (S218 p. 15).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: policy from the relaxation, certified by the same relaxation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: For D-optimal design the relaxation is rounded greedily and its own bound gives the gap.

transferable: Carry a vector technique to matrices by pairing objects: binary vector with projection matrix, perspective with matrix perspective, hull of binaries with {0 <= Y <= I, tr Y <= k} (pp. 3-4, 12-13).
Prove a matrix reformulation by reducing to commuting matrices and eigenvalues, where the scalar result applies (pp. 13-14).
State that a relaxation is the convex hull of a substructure, so readers see where its strength comes from (Theorem 2, pp. 14-15).
Open with the familiar vector problem and its relaxations set beside the new matrix problem (pp. 2-4).
Use a new lower bound to certify existing heuristics, with a gap per instance (pp. 28-30).
coauthors: Ryan Cory-Wright (MIT ORC; PhD 2022 per 04-mentorship.md), Jean Pauphilet (London Business School; PhD 2020 per 04-mentorship.md)

quotes.text: In spite of this progress, almost no equivalent progress has been made on developing strong lower bounds for low-rank problems.
This suggests that heuristic approaches may not maintain their dominance going forward, and motivates the exploration of tight yet affordable relaxations of low-rank problems.

title: Robust convex optimization: A new perspective that unifies and extends
contribution: A general safe-approximation scheme for robust convex constraints with convex uncertainty sets: a conjugate-based bilinear reformulation plus a Reformulation-Perspectification-Technique hierarchy that recovers Bertsimas-Sim, Roos et al. and the S-lemma as special cases, adds lower bounds and probabilistic guarantees, and tightens existing approximations on control and geometric-optimization examples.
problem_entry: {RO; CP as engine} Robust convex constraints require maximizing a convex function, so exact tractable reformulations are out of reach in general, and existing safe approximations cover only homogeneous functions, norm sets or polyhedral sets; the paper seeks one procedure for general convex h and convex Z (p. 3).
key_idea: Write h as its biconjugate to get a robust linear constraint over a lifted non-convex set with bilinear equalities, convexify that set by multiplying pairs of constraints (RPT) into nested approximations, and take robust counterparts via support functions (pp. 6-13).
assumptions: Uncertainty set and conjugate domain each described by linear plus convex inequalities, with as many linear ones as possible (Assumptions 1-2, p. 8); non-negative orthant for the perspectification case, via shifting or lifting (Assumption 3, pp. 15, 28-29); sub-Gaussian coordinates for probabilistic guarantees (Assumption 4, p. 32); test cases: constrained LQ control (N = 20) and random robust geometric programs (100 variables and constraints, L = 6-20, 10 instances) (pp. 21-25).
proof_devices: conjugate-based bilinear reformulation of a robust convex constraint as a robust linear one over a lifted set (Proposition 1, p. 7)
Reformulation-Perspectification-Technique: products of constraint pairs, linear-convex through perspectives, giving nested outer sets (Proposition 2, pp. 8-11)
support-function robust counterparts of intersected sets (p. 13)

recovery of Bertsimas-Sim for homogeneous h and of Roos et al. (static and linear decision rules) as special cases, exact for piecewise-linear h via optimality of linear decision rules on simplices (pp. 15-19)
recovery of the S-lemma and approximate S-lemma for robust quadratics over ellipsoids (p. 19)
perspectification lemma generalizing sub-additivity, and a priori and a posteriori violation bounds via robust complexity (Lemma 1, Propositions 4-5, pp. 29-33)
lower bounds by alternating worst-case scenario generation over the two blocks of a disjoint bilinear problem (pp. 19-21)
experiments: LQ control against the exact SDP reformulation: lifting beats shifting at low to moderate gamma, level-3 approximations within 5% at a fraction of the cost (pp. 22-23); robust geometric programming against a scenario lower bound: the new levels give smaller gaps than the box-based (Roos et al.) and Bertsimas-Sim approaches at similar effort, lifting halves gaps at more than twice the effort, the extra LMI adds nothing (pp. 25-27); no solver, version, machine or code named in the text.
positioning: Unifies and extends Bertsimas-Sim 2006, Zhen et al. and Roos et al. and the S-lemma (pp. 3-4, 15-19); builds on Zhen-De Moor-den Hertog's RPT (p. 6) and Bertsimas-Goyal on linear decision rules (p. 15).
writing: The title states the claim; a three-step recipe (p. 6); an explicit methodological maxim: robustify the nonlinear inequality first, then reformulate it conically (p. 5); open questions flagged (pp. 13, 15).
limits_future: A higher level need not be strictly tighter (p. 11); the LMI's cost-benefit is open (pp. 12-13); no per-level approximation guarantee, called an interesting future direction (p. 15); requires explicit descriptions of the uncertainty set and the conjugate's domain (p. 3).

method_links.note: A hard robust convex constraint becomes an exact robust linear one and is approximated within the original cones (perspectives and conjugates stay in the same or dual cone); boundaries printed.
The a priori violation bound depends on the uncertainty set alone, carrying the Bertsimas-Sim bound device to general convex h; the set size gamma is the knob varied in section 5.
Every safe approximation is reported with a gap against an exact SDP or a scenario lower bound, but there is no exact solve and no stated solver, machine or time limit.
The LMI's null result is printed in the body.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The title's claim; Bertsimas-Sim, Roos et al. (static and linear decision rules) and the S-lemma are recovered as special cases before tighter levels are added.
Nested approximations come from multiplying constraint pairs of increasing type: linear with linear, linear with convex, convex with convex.

transferable: Turn a robust convex constraint into a robust linear one through the conjugate; then only the lifted uncertainty set needs convexifying (pp. 6-7, 13).
Describe the uncertainty set with as many linear inequalities as possible, even redundant ones such as a box around a ball, because RPT multiplies them with the other constraints (pp. 8, 21-22).
Make a set non-negative by shifting or by lifting z = z+ - z-, and compare both numerically (pp. 21-24).
Bound from below by alternating worst-case scenarios on the two blocks of a disjoint bilinear problem, and report each approximation's gap to that bound (pp. 19-21, 25).
